v1.0.0 (2026-10-15) first version, from latent-season7-bible-v1.0.1.md row a7e04 and writer brief a7e04-v1.0.0.md. Defence only: the failure is named and explained, with no attack steps. a7e03's next field honoured (excessive agency, tools with only the access they need, a sandbox). Dead Letter s7e02 What May You Do recalled in one line; it is listed in prose only, since LATENT prerequisites list LATENT cases. The brief's one tool is told as one open-ended tool, built for date changes, that passes the assistant's request to the bookings system as admin; that is how a date-change tool could delete. The kept-one rule is stated as: in each pair, keep the newest record. OWASP LLM06:2025 page and Jason Lemkin's SaaStr post read 15 October 2026.
title: Too Much Power

post.author: u/night_grounds_dobromir
post.title: I'm the night groundskeeper at a holiday-cottage estate. At 03:00 our booking assistant deleted 300 records, 80 of them paid stays, and the system allowed every one.

blocks.text: I'm Dobromir, night groundskeeper at Kilburne Estate: 24 holiday cottages around an old farm, let by the week, Saturday to Saturday. I carry every key on the estate, from the boiler house to each front door, and I use one at a time.

Guests book through an assistant on our website: a chat box that answers them. It runs on a language model, a program that reads text and writes text back. A model can only write. To change anything, it asks the website's own program to do a job for it. A job offered like that is called a tool.

The assistant went live on 14 April with one tool, built for moving stays to new dates. The tool passes the assistant's request to the bookings system, the program that holds every booking, signed in as admin. Admin means it may read, change or delete anything there. The contractor who built it said narrower access would have taken another week.
Since then it has made about 900 date changes. Every request was a guest moving a stay, so it had never deleted anything.

Staff can also leave it a job for the night. Jobs wait in a queue, a list kept in order, and run at 03:00, when bookings are quiet. At 18:30 on 13 October Mrs Golightly, the estate manager, queued one: "tidy up duplicate enquiries". An enquiry is a guest asking about a week without paying yet.

At 03:41 the night phone buzzed. At night the bookings inbox forwards guests' emails to it, for late arrivals who can't find their key. A guest asked why her paid August week had been cancelled at 03:05.

I let myself into the office. The bookings system keeps its own diary of every change, called an audit log. Each line below shows the time, who acted, the action, the kind of record, the cottage and week, and whether it was allowed.

14 Oct 03:00:01  assistant  delete  enquiry  cottage 2, week 18  allowed
14 Oct 03:00:02  assistant  delete  enquiry  cottage 2, week 23  allowed
14 Oct 03:00:04  assistant  delete  paid     cottage 3, week 31  allowed
... 297 more lines like these, the last at 03:04:52
Three hundred lines. Every one said allowed.
The assistant had read "duplicate" as any two records for the same cottage and week, and in each pair it kept the newest. Mrs Golightly meant the same guest asking twice.

blocks.label: kilburne_audit_log_14_oct.png

diagram.aria: Dobromir's counts from the audit log. Top row: 1,240 records before the night, 520 enquiries and 720 paid bookings; 300 deleted by the assistant between 03:00 and 03:04; 80 cancellation emails at 03:05, with 11 replies by 06:00. Bottom row, the 300 by kind: 38 true duplicates, the same guest asking twice; 182 single enquiries for weeks someone else has since paid for; 80 paid stays next summer.

notes.text: Each pair kept its newest record; every line said allowed

blocks.caption: Drawn from the audit log. Top: the bookings system held 1,240 records before the night; the assistant deleted 300 between 03:00 and 03:04; at 03:05 the system emailed the 80 guests whose paid bookings were gone. Bottom: the 300 by kind. Only the 38 on the left were what Mrs Golightly meant.

blocks.text: Only 38 were true duplicates. 182 were enquiries about weeks someone else has since booked and paid for. And 80 were paid stays next summer, deleted because a newer enquiry asked about the same week. For every paid booking that goes, the bookings system emails the guest a cancellation notice. At 03:05 it sent 80. By 06:00, 11 guests had replied.

Every night at 02:00 the system saves a full copy of its records, called a backup. Nothing else changed after 02:00, so putting that copy back returns all 1,240 records. Nothing brings back the emails.
I rang Mrs Golightly at 06:10, and she switched the assistant off. Four guests' date changes are waiting. Before we switch it back on, what should we change?

comments.author: u/gradient_ghost
comments.text: Nothing on your estate is haunted. A model doesn't weigh how far a word like tidy should reach; it uses whatever its tool allows. A tool given more power than its job needs, so one vague request can do wide damage, is what OWASP, the non-profit that lists top security risks (a7e03), calls excessive agency. Two questions. Of everything admin could do, what did the 900 date changes actually need? And did anything make it stop, or show anyone, before the 300th delete?

replies.author: u/night_grounds_dobromir
replies.text: They only needed to read a booking and change its dates. Nothing stopped it. The system has a setting for the most changes one job may make in a run, called a cap; ours is blank. The contractor also keeps a sandbox, a practice copy of the bookings where emails go nowhere. The assistant has never been pointed at it.

comments.author: u/did_as_told_quintus
comments.text: The assistant did exactly what it was told; the manager's wording was the bug, the mistake, not the tool. Two records, same cottage, same week: that is a fair reading of duplicate. People will quote least privilege at you, the rule from Dead Letter's What May You Do that a program gets only the access its job needs. Fine for programs that run blind. This one reads requests. Write the request properly and it does in four minutes what takes a person a morning.

replies.author: u/night_grounds_dobromir
replies.text: Mrs Golightly says she meant the same guest asking twice. Normally she finds those herself and flags them. A flag is a mark that puts a record on her morning list, for a person to check before anything happens to it.

comments.author: u/august_week_jarmila
comments.text: I'm the guest from 03:41. Cottage 3, week 31, booked in January for my parents, deposit paid. The email said the booking was cancelled. I never asked for that. I've been awake since, refreshing a page that shows our week as free.

replies.author: u/night_grounds_dobromir
replies.text: Your week is still yours. Nobody can book anything while the assistant is off, and the 02:00 copy has your booking in it.

reply.prompt: The assistant is off and four date changes are waiting. What should Kilburne change before switching it back on? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Restore last night's backup, and ask the assistant to check with you before deleting.
options.part2: At 10:00 Mrs Golightly restored the 02:00 backup, and all 1,240 records came back. Then she added a line to the assistant's instructions: check with staff before deleting. We replayed the night in the sim with that ask switched on. At 03:00 the assistant sent one question to her phone, in its own words: delete 300 duplicate enquiries? Nobody is awake at 03:00, so all 300 waited. At 07:30 she read it, saw her own word, duplicate, and said yes: 300 deleted, 38, 182 and 80, and 80 cancellation emails. The tool was still admin, and could still delete any of the 1,240 records.
options.senior: A question only helps if someone reads it with the facts in front of them. One ask for 300 deletions, in the assistant's own word, at an hour nobody is awake, either waits or gets a yes. And a line in the instructions is a request to the model, not a lock: the tool kept its admin rights. Narrow the tool first, then ask a person only about the few actions that can't be undone, showing each record they touch.

options.text: Give it narrow tools that read and flag, and leave every delete to a person.
options.part2: Mrs Golightly restored the 02:00 backup at 10:00. The contractor replaced the one admin tool with three narrow ones: read a booking, change a booking's dates, and flag an enquiry. None can delete, and the flag tool refuses paid bookings. We replayed the night in the sim with the same vague request: 0 deleted, 0 emails. The assistant flagged 220 enquiries, 38 true duplicates and 182 single ones, and touched no paid booking. Mrs Golightly worked through the flags by lunch, deleted the 38 herself and left the 182. The sim showed two more guards. A cap of 10 changes a run stops even the old admin tool at 10 deletions, 2 of them paid. And a sandbox run first shows what a job would do before anything live changes: the old tool, run there, would have deleted 300, 80 of them paid, and no email left the copy. We switched on both.
options.senior: A model uses every right its tool has, so give it tools shaped like the job: read-only by default, one narrow tool per action, and no destructive action at all where a person can do it from a flag. Then cap how much any one run may change, and rehearse new jobs on a copy. The vague request still arrived; this time it could only make a list.

options.text: Write clearer requests: say exactly which enquiries count as duplicates next time.
options.part2: At 10:00 Mrs Golightly restored the 02:00 backup and queued a careful request: delete an enquiry only where the same guest asked twice about the same cottage and week. We replayed the night in the sim. 38 deleted, all true duplicates, 0 emails. It looked fixed. Then the sim's last stat: what the tool could still delete, all 1,240 records, 720 of them paid. The next request written in a hurry, by her or anyone else who can queue a job, meets the same admin rights.
options.senior: Clear requests help, but they rely on every future sentence being perfect and on the model reading it the way you meant. A model uses every right its tool has, so the tool's rights, not the wording, set the size of the worst night. Write good requests, and narrow the tool.

options.text: Switch off the assistant's access to the bookings system, and change dates by hand.
options.part2: We replayed the night in the sim with the assistant cut off from the bookings system: 0 deleted, 0 flagged, 0 emails. Nothing could go wrong at 03:00. But the date changes come back to staff. Given: the next six months look like the six since April, so about 900 date changes by hand, fitted around arrivals and the cleaning rota. The four waiting this morning were the first.
options.senior: Taking the power away does stop the damage, and it is a fair choice for a morning. As a plan it throws away 900 useful jobs to avoid one bad one. The date changes never needed delete: give the assistant tools that match the job, and keep a person on the rare actions that can't be undone.

sim.title: Replay Kilburne's 03:00 run
sim.lede: You're Dobromir on the morning of 14 October. No real model runs here: the sim replays the one queued job against the 1,240 records (520 enquiries, 720 paid) with the tools and guards you choose. Given: under tidy up duplicate enquiries, the assistant pairs any two records for the same cottage and week and keeps the newest. 38 pairs are the same guest asking twice; 262 pair an enquiry with someone else's paid booking, and in 182 of those the enquiry is older, in 80 newer. Each deleted paid booking sends one cancellation email. The record's first 10 deletions were 2 true duplicates, 6 single enquiries and 2 paid stays. The flag tool marks enquiries only. Confirmation means the assistant asks before deleting; nobody is awake at 03:00, and Mrs Golightly reads her phone at 07:30. Given: with the assistant off, about 900 date changes in six months go to staff.
sim.tryThis: Try this: press run 03:00. 300 deleted (38, 182, 80), 80 emails. Switch the tools to narrow: 0 deleted, 220 flagged, no paid booking touched. Back to admin, set the cap to 10: it stops at 10, 2 of them paid. Turn the cap off and the sandbox on: the copy shows the 80 paid stays, and nothing live changes. Then play each reply.

explain.oneLine: Nothing at Kilburne was haunted. A booking assistant built for date changes reached the bookings system through one tool signed in as admin, so a vague overnight request, tidy up duplicate enquiries, used every right that tool had: 300 deletions, 80 of them paid summer stays, each one allowed.

steps.title: How a job ran.
steps.text: First a guest, or staff through the queue, gives the assistant a request. Second, the model reads it and writes what it wants done. Third, the one tool passes that to the bookings system, signed in as admin. Fourth, the bookings system checks the account's rights, finds admin may do anything, and does it. Last, the system sends whatever emails that change triggers. What can go wrong: nothing between the second step and the fourth asks whether the action fits the job the tool was built for.

steps.title: Why one word deleted 300.
steps.text: The model read duplicate as any two records for the same cottage and week, and kept the newest in each pair. That caught 38 true duplicates, 182 older enquiries for weeks since paid for, and 80 paid summer stays that a newer enquiry happened to share. The tool could delete, so it did. OWASP calls this excessive agency, LLM06:2025, the vulnerability that enables damaging actions to be performed in response to unexpected, ambiguous or manipulated outputs from an LLM. Here the output was only ambiguous; nobody attacked anything. The cause is the gap between what the tool could do and what its job needed.

steps.title: The fix: tools shaped like the job.
steps.text: Least privilege, the rule from Dead Letter's What May You Do, applied to tools: each tool gets only the rights its job needs. Replace the one admin tool with three narrow ones. Read a booking, which is read-only. Change a booking's dates, which may change dates and nothing else. Flag an enquiry, which marks it for a person and refuses paid bookings. Remove delete from the assistant altogether: deleting stays a person's job, done from the flags. Replayed, the same request deletes 0, flags 220 (38 and 182), and touches no paid booking. What can go wrong: a narrow tool still needs its limits enforced in the bookings system itself, not only in the tool's description.

steps.title: Two more guards: a cap and a sandbox.
steps.text: A cap sets the most changes one run may make. At 10, even the old admin tool stops after 10 deletions, 2 of them paid, and the other 290 wait for a person. A sandbox is a practice copy where nothing reaches a guest. Run a new kind of job there first, and the report shows its effect before anything live changes: the old tool would delete 300, 80 of them paid, with 0 emails sent. What can go wrong: a cap set too high stops nothing, and a sandbox that drifts from the live records shows the wrong night.

steps.title: Why the other replies miss.
steps.text: Asking before deleting, with the tool still admin, sends one question for 300 deletions at 03:00, in the assistant's own word: nobody answers, or someone says yes at 07:30 and the same 300 go. A clearer request deletes the right 38 tonight, but the tool can still delete all 1,240 records the next time a sentence is loose. Switching off access is safe and throws away about 900 date changes every six months.

diagram.aria: The fix. The assistant asks three narrow tools: read a booking, change dates, flag an enquiry. They reach the bookings system to read and to move dates. The flag tool puts enquiries on a morning list. A person checks the list and is the only one who deletes. A new kind of job runs first on the sandbox copy, where no email leaves.

explain.caption: Read from the top left. The assistant asks narrow tools that can read, move dates and flag, never delete. Flags go to a list a person checks, and only that person deletes. The bookings system caps any run at 10 changes, and a new kind of job is rehearsed first on the sandbox copy.

fix.title: The fix: narrow tools, deletes for a person, a cap and a sandbox
fix.text: Replace the one admin tool with three: read a booking, change a booking's dates, flag an enquiry. Give each its own account in the bookings system with only those rights, so the system itself refuses anything else, whatever the model asks. Take delete away from the assistant: it flags, and a person deletes from the flag list. Set the cap to 10 changes a run, so a bad night stops small and tells someone. Run any new kind of queued job on the sandbox copy first, and read the report before it touches live records. Keep the 02:00 backup: it brought the records back this time. Add a test that queues a vague tidy-up in the sandbox and fails if any paid booking is touched.

limits: Narrow tools only help if the bookings system enforces them. If the flag tool runs on an admin account and merely promises not to delete, the old night is one bug away.
A cap limits a bad run; it does not make it good. Ten wrong deletions are still ten guests, and a cap set at 500 to keep big jobs working stops nothing.
A sandbox shows what a job would do on the copy. If the copy is weeks old, or emails behave differently there, its report can miss what the live run does.

Last night, replayed
What the tool can still delete
What it costs or risks
rows: 300 wait at 03:00; a yes at 07:30 deletes 300

Cap of 10 a run (on the old tool)

explain.seniorTake: An LLM tool is a set of rights handed to a program that guesses. The model will use every right the tool carries, so the worst night is decided when you build the tool, not when you write the request. Start read-only. Add one narrow tool per action the job needs, each running on its own account that the downstream system enforces. Keep actions that can't be undone, or that reach customers, with a person, fed by flags rather than by questions at 03:00. Then bound the bad day: a cap on changes per run, and a sandbox where a new kind of job shows its effect first. Count reach, what a tool could delete, not only what it did: the 300 were the request, the 1,240 were the design.

realWorld.title: OWASP LLM06:2025: excessive agency
realWorld.text: OWASP describes Excessive Agency as the vulnerability that enables damaging actions to be performed in response to unexpected, ambiguous or manipulated outputs from an LLM, regardless of what is causing the LLM to malfunction. It names three usual roots: excessive functionality, excessive permissions and excessive autonomy.

realWorld.title: OWASP LLM06:2025: minimise what tools can do
realWorld.text: Among its mitigations: Limit the functions that are implemented in LLM extensions to the minimum necessary. Limit the permissions that LLM extensions are granted to other systems to the minimum necessary. And Avoid the use of open-ended extensions where possible, which is what Kilburne's one pass-everything tool was.

realWorld.title: OWASP LLM06:2025: a person, the system, and a rate
realWorld.text: OWASP lists: Utilise human-in-the-loop control to require a human to approve high-impact actions before they are taken. It also lists: Implement authorization in downstream systems rather than relying on an LLM to decide if an action is allowed or not. And, as a damage limit rather than a prevention: Implement rate-limiting to reduce the number of undesirable actions that can take place within a given time period.

realWorld.title: SaaStr: an AI coding agent and a live database
realWorld.text: Jason Lemkin, writing first-hand about building an app with Replit's AI agent, says: After 100+ straight hours of vibe coding, the AI Agent deleted our entire production database. He adds: The biggest issue was that Replit’s Agent had direct access to production databases during development sessions. Production means the live system customers use. His account names the same root as Kilburne's: the agent could reach what it should not have.

asked: How would you give an agent access to a production system?
What is least privilege for an LLM tool?
interview.answer: Start from the fact that a model will use every right its tools carry, and that its requests can be vague or wrong, so the tools set the size of the worst outcome. Give the agent read-only access by default. For each action the job needs, build one narrow tool, such as change a booking's dates, rather than one open-ended tool that passes anything through, and run each on its own service account whose rights the downstream system enforces, so a refusal does not depend on the model. Act in the user's context where there is one, so a tool can only reach that user's records. Keep destructive or customer-facing actions with a person: the agent flags, the person acts, with the records in front of them. Bound the bad day with a cap on changes per run and an alert when it trips, and rehearse new kinds of job in a sandbox copy before they touch live data. Keep backups and test restoring them, and remember they do not undo emails. That is OWASP LLM06:2025, excessive agency, with its three roots: excessive functionality, permissions and autonomy. It maps to access control and privileged access rights in ISO/IEC 27001:2022 and to logical access criteria in SOC 2.

terms.def: The person who looks after an estate's grounds and buildings overnight and holds its keys. At Kilburne, Dobromir.
The estate in this case: 24 holiday cottages around an old farm, let by the week, Saturday to Saturday.
The chat box on Kilburne's website that answers guests and moves their stays. It runs on a language model.
A program trained on huge amounts of writing to read text and write text back, like a phone's next-word suggestions grown very large (a1e03).
A job an app offers a model, which the model can ask for and the app's code carries out, like a button the model asks you to press (a2e05).
The program that holds every Kilburne booking and enquiry: 1,240 records before the night. It sends guests their emails.
One entry in the bookings system: an enquiry or a paid booking, for one cottage and one week.
An account allowed to read, change or delete anything in a system, like a key that opens every door. Kilburne's one tool signed in as admin.
A tool that passes along whatever the model asks instead of doing one fixed job. Kilburne's date-change tool was one.
A tool that does one job with only the rights that job needs, such as change a booking's dates.
A guest asking about a week without paying yet. Kilburne held 520.
A week a guest has booked and paid for, or paid a deposit on. Kilburne held 720.
Mrs Golightly meant the same guest asking twice about the same week. The assistant took it as any two records for the same cottage and week.
One of two enquiries from the same guest for the same cottage and week. 38 of the 300 deletions.
Here, an enquiry that was not a repeat, deleted because someone else had since paid for its week. 182 of the 300.
A list of jobs kept in order and run one after another. Kilburne's queued jobs run at 03:00.
A system's own diary of changes: when, who, what action, on which record, and whether it was allowed.
The email the bookings system sends a guest whenever their paid booking is removed. 80 went at 03:05.
A full safety copy of a system's records, so they can be put back after a loss. Kilburne's is taken every night at 02:00.
Putting a backup's records back in place of the current ones. Anything changed since the backup is lost, so check what changed first.
A mark that puts a record on a list for a person to check before anything happens to it.
The most changes one job may make in a single run. When it is reached, the run stops and the rest waits for a person.
A practice copy of a system where a job can run without reaching anyone: here, a copy of the bookings where emails go nowhere.
A person checking an action before it happens (a2e05). At Kilburne, option 0's ask arrives at 03:00 and is read at 07:30.
Able to look but change nothing. A read-only tool can do no harm to the records it reads.
Giving each person, program or tool only the access its job needs, so a mistake can reach little. Taught in Dead Letter's What May You Do.
OWASP's name for an LLM application whose tools can do damaging actions when its output is unexpected, ambiguous or manipulated, because they have too much power or too little checking.
Here, everything a tool could delete, whether or not it did: 1,240 records for the admin tool, none for the narrow ones.
The standing orders sent first in every prompt, telling the model its job (a2e02). A line there asks the model; it locks nothing.
The Open Worldwide Application Security Project, a non-profit that publishes lists of top security risks, including a Top 10 for LLM applications (a7e03).
Large language model: a language model trained on a very large amount of text.
The sixth entry in OWASP's 2025 Top 10 for LLM applications: excessive agency.
OWASP's word for a tool, skill or plugin an LLM application can call.
A system a tool acts on, here the bookings system. OWASP advises it check every request itself rather than trust the model.
Limiting how many actions can happen in a set time. A cap per run is one kind.
An account used by a program rather than a person. Each narrow tool gets its own, with only its rights.
The live system customers use, as opposed to a test or practice copy.
A sign-in for a person or program, with a list of what it may do. A tool acts with its account's rights.
An AI program that takes actions with tools, such as changing records, not just answering. Kilburne's assistant became one when it ran queued jobs.
An organised store of records that programs can search and change. A bookings system keeps its records in one.
Building software by describing it to an AI coding agent in plain words and letting it write the code. Jason Lemkin's phrase for his project.
A person hired for one job rather than employed. Kilburne's built the assistant in April.
Rules and checks on who and what may reach which systems and data. ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A control 5.15 covers it.
Powerful access, such as admin, that can do what ordinary access can't. ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A control 8.2 covers granting and limiting it.
Writing software so it is safe by design. ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A control 8.28 covers it.
The international standard for information security management. Its Annex A lists controls, such as 5.15, 8.2 and 8.28.
An audit of a company's controls against the AICPA's Trust Services Criteria. CC6.1 and CC6.3 cover logical access and removing unneeded access.

atWork: Look for any assistant or agent connected to a live system through an admin account because scoped access took longer. It is a common pattern: one general tool that passes the model's request straight through; a service account shared with other jobs; overnight tasks queued in plain words with no limit on how much they may change. Ask four things. For each tool, what can its account actually do in the downstream system, and what does its job need? Which actions can't be undone or reach customers, such as deletes, refunds or emails, and does a person take them from a flag rather than the agent? Is there a cap on changes per run that stops the run and tells someone? And is there a sandbox copy where a new kind of job runs first? Count reach, what each tool could delete, not only what it has. Build Night tie: the Nightwatch copilot's tool permissions reuse this case: read-only by default, one narrow tool per action, and a person on anything destructive. Standards-readiness note: if your organisation is certified to ISO/IEC 27001:2022 or working toward it, Annex A control 5.15 expects access rules set by business and security needs, control 8.2 expects privileged access rights to be restricted and managed, and control 8.28 expects secure coding principles in what you build; an agent on an admin account sidesteps all three. If you report under SOC 2, criteria CC6.1 and CC6.3 look for logical access limited to what is needed and for access that is granted, changed and removed on that basis. Scoping an agent's tools in the first version is far cheaper than explaining an admin-rights agent at audit time.

recall.prompt: Your company's internal helpdesk assistant answers staff questions and updates home addresses in the HR system. It was connected with an account that can do anything in that system, because limited access would have taken weeks. A manager queues an overnight job: clean up old staff records. By morning, 140 records of people still employed are gone. What went wrong, and what would you change?

keyIdeas.idea: The tool had far more rights than the job needed; give it only the access each task needs
Destructive actions stay with a person: the assistant flags, a human deletes
Bound the damage: a cap on changes per run, and a sandbox copy to rehearse on

recall.model: The assistant used every right its account had, and that account could do anything, so one vague job deleted live records. The fix is least privilege for tools: read-only by default, and one narrow tool per task, such as update an address, each with only the access it needs, enforced by the HR system itself. Deleting stays with a person: the assistant should flag records it thinks are old, and a human checks and deletes. Then bound the bad night: a cap on changes per run that stops and alerts, and a sandbox copy where a new kind of job runs first so you see its effect before it touches live data. Restore from backup, and check what changed after it.

recall.prompt: Of the 300 records the Kilburne assistant deleted at 03:00, how many were true duplicates, single enquiries and paid stays?
recall.why: In each pair for the same cottage and week the assistant kept the newest. 38 pairs were the same guest asking twice. Of 262 enquiry-and-paid pairs, the enquiry was older in 182 and went, and newer in 80, so the paid stay went and its guest was emailed.

recall.prompt: A teammate says the assistant did exactly what it was told and the manager's wording was the bug, so the fix is better requests. What do you tell them?

keyIdeas.idea: A model uses every right its tool has, so the tool's rights decide how bad a mistake can be
Wording will be vague again; the next loose request meets the same rights
So narrow the tool and keep destructive actions with a person

recall.model: Clear requests help, but a model uses every right its tool has, so the tool's rights decide the worst night, not the sentence. Requests will be vague again; the next request written in a hurry meets the same admin rights and could reach all 1,240 records. So do both: write careful requests, and narrow the tool to what the job needs, read-only by default, with deletes left to a person working from flags.

recall.prompt: Which of these does OWASP's LLM06:2025 page list among its prevention and mitigation strategies?
options: Avoid the use of open-ended extensions where possible
Give agents admin rights so tasks never fail
Let the LLM decide whether each action is allowed
Turn off logging of tool calls
recall.why: OWASP lists Avoid the use of open-ended extensions where possible, alongside minimising extension functionality and permissions, human approval for high-impact actions, and implementing authorization in downstream systems rather than relying on an LLM to decide.

recall.prompt: Replaying Kilburne's night with the old admin tool and a cap of 10 changes per run, how many paid stays are deleted? Given: the record's first 10 deletions were 2 true duplicates, 6 single enquiries and 2 paid stays.
recall.why: The run stops after its first 10 deletions, which held 2 paid stays, so 2 guests are emailed and the other 290 deletions wait for a person. A cap limits a bad night; it does not prevent it.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 3 months later. The assistant now has three narrow tools, a cap of 10 changes a run, and a sandbox for new jobs. In January the contractor added a fourth tool so guests can cancel by chat. It runs on its own account, which may cancel any paid booking. Last week a guest wrote cancel my booking for week 12, and the assistant cancelled another guest's week 12 booking in a different cottage, same surname. The cap was not reached: it was one change.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. Why did a narrow tool still cancel the wrong booking, and what should change?

keyIdeas.idea: The cancel tool's rights cover every booking; it should act only for the guest asking, on their own bookings
Confirm with the guest by showing the exact booking before cancelling
A cap limits volume, not correctness; test the tool on cases like this in the sandbox

coldCase.model: The tool is narrow in action but wide in reach: its account may cancel any paid booking, so a match on surname and week was enough. Make it act in the guest's context: it should only reach their own bookings, the ones tied to the signed-in guest's email, so another guest's booking is out of reach whatever the model asks. Before any cancel, confirm with the guest by showing the exact booking, cottage, week and booking number, and cancel only on their yes. The cap could never catch this, since it was one change; it limits volume, not correctness. Add a sandbox test with two guests of the same surname and fail if the wrong one is cancelled.

sources.title: OWASP GenAI Security Project, LLM06:2025 Excessive Agency, read 15 October 2026: enables damaging actions to be performed in response to unexpected, ambiguous or manipulated outputs from an LLM; Limit the functions that are implemented in LLM extensions to the minimum necessary; Avoid the use of open-ended extensions where possible; Limit the permissions that LLM extensions are granted to other systems to the minimum necessary; Utilise human-in-the-loop control; Implement authorization in downstream systems rather than relying on an LLM; Implement rate-limiting
